notes: Interlocutory Daie homelessness appeal; Longmore LJ grants permission to apply for judicial review after fresh Camden letter.

enrichment.short_title: Daie v Camden: permission to apply for judicial review on fresh homeless application
key_facts: Dr Daie challenged Camden's handling of his homelessness application and sought permission to appeal after Hodge J's earlier judgment.
Keene LJ had adjourned the permission application; a letter dated 6 October 2004 refusing a fresh application had not been before him.
Camden refused to consider a fresh application of 10 September 2004 on the basis that there had been no material change of circumstances.
The Court of Appeal considered whether that refusal letter was consistent with Tower Hamlets v Rikha Begum.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal from Hodge J's judgment, converted under CPR 52.15(3) into permission to apply for judicial review.
enrichment.outcome: Adjournment refused; permission to apply for judicial review granted; Camden ordered to continue temporary accommodation; expedition and skeleton directions made.
enrichment.ratio: Where a local authority's fresh refusal letter on a homelessness application was not before the judge on an earlier permission application and raises a question of law under recent Court of Appeal authority, permission to apply for judicial review may properly be granted under CPR 52.15(3).
legal_issues: Whether Camden's 6 October 2004 letter was a decision on the September 2004 homeless application
Whether the letter's wording complied with Rikha Begum on fresh applications
Whether permission to appeal or judicial review was the appropriate route
Whether interim accommodation should continue pending judicial review
linked_authorities: London Borough of Tower Hamlets v Rikha Begum [2005] EWCA Civ 340

confidence.notes: Short interlocutory judgment; procedural orders and legal basis are clear though underlying merits were not finally decided.

notes: Earlier Daie interlocutory hearing; Keene LJ adjourns permission application and preserves interim housing.

enrichment.short_title: Daie v Camden: adjournment of permission appeal and interim accommodation
key_facts: Dr Daie applied for permission to appeal in homelessness proceedings against Camden.
Keene LJ noted a Part 7 application dated 10 September 2004 that appeared not to have been addressed in the papers.
The challenged letter of 6 October 2004 appeared to concern temporary accommodation at Adamson Road rather than the September application.
Camden was not represented at the hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application for permission to appeal adjourned on notice to Camden.
enrichment.outcome: Application adjourned to 31 March 2005 on notice to Camden; Camden ordered to continue providing housing accommodation until that hearing; urgent transcript of Hodge J's judgment directed.
enrichment.ratio: Where papers before the court do not appear to address a live Part 7 homelessness application and the local authority is absent, an adjournment on notice with interim accommodation is appropriate so the authority can assist on the merits.
legal_issues: Whether the 6 October 2004 letter was a decision on the September 2004 homeless application
Whether interim accommodation should be preserved pending permission
Whether Camden should be heard before permission is determined

confidence.notes: Brief procedural ruling with clear directions; substantive homelessness issues reserved.

notes: Medical negligence limitation trial; Hodge J holds claim against NHS Trust in time under section 14 and would exercise section 33 discretion.

enrichment.short_title: Martin v Kaisary: limitation and joinder of NHS Trust after prostate surgery
key_facts: Mr Martin underwent a private radical prostatectomy by Mr Kaisary at the Royal Free Hospital in October 2000.
Post-operative internal bleeding went unchecked and he suffered a cardiac arrest causing permanent brain damage.
Proceedings were issued against the surgeon within three years but the NHS Trust was not joined until after the limitation period.
Mr Martin believed until after August 2001 that Heparin/Enoxaparin caused the bleeding rather than negligent post-operative monitoring.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary issue trial on whether the claim against the proposed second defendant NHS Trust was barred by the Limitation Act.
enrichment.outcome: Claim against the Trust held in time on section 14 date of knowledge; court indicated it would also have allowed the action to proceed under section 33.
enrichment.ratio: A claimant who reasonably investigates the wrong cause of a post-operative injury and is 'barking up the wrong tree' may lack section 14 knowledge of attributable negligence by hospital staff until later expert evidence; solicitor error in failing to join the Trust does not necessarily bar the claim.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Martin had section 14 knowledge of negligence attributable to NHS staff before 5 August 2001
Whether the Spargo 'wrong tree' principle applied
Whether section 33 discretion should permit joinder despite solicitor delay
Whether CPR 19.5 justified adding the Trust as a necessary party
linked_authorities: North Essex District Health Authority v Spargo [1997] 8 Med LR 125
Das v Ganju [1999] Lloyd's Rep Med 198
Steed v Peverel [2001] EWCA Civ 419

confidence.notes: Detailed findings on limitation and explicit section 33 analysis provide a clear basis for enrichment.

notes: Youth court committal challenge; Laws LJ dismisses JR though district judge's reasons were inadequate on W and K guidance.

enrichment.short_title: C v Leeds Youth Court: committal for trial on Class A drug supply charges
key_facts: C, aged 14 at the time of the offences, was charged with being concerned in the supply of heroin on two occasions in Chapeltown, Leeds.
District Judge Kitson declined youth court jurisdiction and committed C and co-accused to the Crown Court.
The prosecution case included test purchase operations with C acting as lookout or directing officers to a supply location.
C argued committal was wrong because there was no real prospect of a section 91 detention sentence of two years or more.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited judicial review of a youth court decision to decline jurisdiction and commit a 14-year-old for trial.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; despite inadequate reasons, only one outcome was realistically available because there was a real prospect of detention of two years or more.
enrichment.ratio: Youth court committal under section 24 requires a real prospect that section 91 long-term detention may be passed; inadequate reasons may justify quashing only if more than one outcome was open, but here the seriousness of Class A supply offending against W and K and H, A and O guidance meant committal was the only available conclusion.
legal_issues: Whether there was a real prospect of a section 91 sentence of two years or more
Whether the district judge applied W and K and H, A and O guidance
Whether reasons for declining jurisdiction were adequate
Whether C's role as lookout made the case less grave than Khalid Hussain
linked_authorities: W and K [2002] EWHC Admin 164
H, A and O [2004] EWHC Admin 2912
R v Khalid Hussain [2001] 2 Cr App R (S) 273
R v Sheffield Youth Court [2003] EWHC Admin 309

confidence.notes: Statutory framework, guidance and final disposition are clearly reasoned despite procedural reasons challenge.

notes: Litigant-in-person grant refusal appeal; Tugendhat J upholds strike-out of negligence and misrepresentation claim against NDC.

enrichment.short_title: Iakovlev v NDC: strike-out of discretionary grant funding claim
key_facts: Mr Iakovlev, a former Russian journalist, applied to EC1 New Deal for Communities for funding for a 'Christmas Wish Website' project for children.
NDC refused funding in June 2003 citing ethos, funding gap, cultural sensitivity and management concerns.
He claimed damages for negligence, misrepresentation and fraud after encouragement in a March 2003 letter from NDC staff.
Master Fontaine struck out the claim; he applied for permission to appeal as a litigant in person.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal from summary strike-out under CPR 3.4 and 24.2.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; no duty of care or contractual entitlement to compensation arose from refusal of a discretionary grant.
enrichment.ratio: A body distributing discretionary government grants owes no common law duty of care entitling unsuccessful applicants to damages for time spent on applications; encouragement to apply does not create enforceable rights to funding, though public law fairness duties may exist without a damages remedy of the kind claimed.
legal_issues: Whether NDC owed a duty of care in assessing grant applications
Whether encouragement letters gave rise to misrepresentation or fraud claims
Whether judicial review rather than damages was the appropriate remedy
Whether the Master showed bias or failed to address the claimant's points

confidence.notes: Master's reasoning and Tugendhat J's permission refusal are explicit on all pleaded causes of action.

notes: Same-sex family appeal; Court of Appeal grants shared residence and parental responsibility to former cohabiting partner.

enrichment.short_title: Re G (Children): shared residence and parental responsibility for same-sex partner
area_of_law: Trusts of land and family property
key_facts: Miss W cohabited with Miss G from 1995 to 2003; two children were born to Miss G by anonymous donor insemination.
Miss W sought a joint residence order to acquire parental responsibility, which section 4 did not confer on her as a non-biological parent.
CAFCASS recommended shared residence; the trial judge refused joint residence but made detailed contact and specific issue orders.
The judge found Miss G's planned move to Cornwall was partly designed to frustrate contact.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal of shared residence and parental responsibility after a contested county court hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; joint residence order granted conferring parental responsibility on Miss W.
enrichment.ratio: Where a same-sex co-parent has played a central role in children's lives and the primary carer seeks to marginalise her, a joint residence order may be required to safeguard the children's welfare; rejection of CAFCASS recommendations requires cogent reasons, especially where the judge finds manoeuvring to exclude the applicant.
legal_issues: Whether a joint residence order was in the children's best interests
Whether the judge adequately reasoned departure from CAFCASS recommendation
Whether parental responsibility was necessary to prevent marginalisation
Application of family diversity authorities to same-sex co-parenting
linked_authorities: A v A (Shared Residence) [2004] 1 FLR 1195
Re H [1991] Fam 151
Re C and V [1998] 1 FLR 392
Fitzpatrick v Sterling Housing Association Ltd [2001] 1 AC 27
Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza [2004] 3 WLR 113

confidence.notes: Detailed appellate reasoning on welfare, parental responsibility and CAFCASS departure is comprehensive.

notes: Late entrapment appeal dismissed; Edwards and Lewis Article 6 finding did not render 1996 guilty pleas unsafe.

enrichment.short_title: R v Lewis: unsafe conviction appeal after Edwards and Lewis
key_facts: Mr Lewis pleaded guilty in 1996 to three counts of custody of counterfeit currency with intent after undercover police operations.
He unsuccessfully sought a stay for entrapment and challenged PII disclosure before pleading guilty.
The European Court in Edwards and Lewis v UK (2003) found Article 6 breach in the PII/entrapment procedure.
He appealed conviction very late, arguing the Strasbourg finding made his convictions unsafe.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge with a very long extension of time.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; convictions not unsafe despite Strasbourg unfairness finding; certification of point of law refused.
enrichment.ratio: A Strasbourg Article 6 finding of unfair PII procedure does not automatically render pre-HRA convictions unsafe; where the appellant pleaded guilty with full knowledge of disclosed evidence, possessed counterfeit notes on arrest, and the trial judge's entrapment ruling was based on disclosed tapes, the convictions may remain safe.
legal_issues: Whether Edwards and Lewis made the convictions unsafe
Whether entrapment and PII procedure amounted to abuse of process
Retrospective effect of HRA 1998 after Lambert and Kansal
Whether guilty plea precluded appeal after Chalkley v Jeffries
linked_authorities: Edwards and Lewis v United Kingdom (2003) 15 BHRC 189
Looseley [2001] 1 WLR 2060
Chalkley v Jeffries [1998] 2 Cr App R 79
R v Lambert [2002] 2 AC 545
R v H and C [2004] 2 AC 174

confidence.notes: Appellate reasoning on safety, HRA retrospectivity and guilty plea effect is explicit.

notes: Attorney General reference; community order for assault with intent to rob and domestic ABH increased to three years.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference No 147 of 2004: unduly lenient robbery and domestic violence sentences
key_facts: The offender pleaded guilty to assault occasioning ABH on a former partner, assault with intent to rob, and common assault.
He breached an injunction, attacked Paula Millington at her home while their child was present, and separately robbed an Afghan student with punches and a knife.
HHJ Fish imposed a two-year community rehabilitation order with a domestic violence programme.
The offender subsequently failed to comply with probation appointments.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 alleging unduly lenient sentences.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; sentences quashed and replaced with a total of three years' imprisonment after double jeopardy adjustment.
enrichment.ratio: Save in wholly exceptional circumstances, immediate custody is the normal sentence for robbery involving violence and a lethal weapon; a community order for such offences together with a serious domestic ABH in breach of an injunction was unduly lenient.
legal_issues: Whether the community order was unduly lenient for assault with intent to rob
Aggravating features of domestic ABH in breach of an injunction
Effect of double jeopardy on the substituted sentence
Impact of post-sentence non-compliance with probation

Attorney General's Reference No 105 of 2002 [2003] 2 Cr App R (S) 319
Attorney General's Reference Nos 150 and 151 of 2002 [2003] 2 Cr App R (S) 658
Attorney General's Reference No 64 of 2003 [2004] 2 Cr App R (S) 106

notes: Pinfield v Eagles care-home dispute; beneficial shares declared 39:61 and fraudulent Companies House steps invalidated.

enrichment.short_title: Pinfield v Eagles: beneficial ownership of care home companies
key_facts: Mrs Pinfield and Mr Eagles jointly pursued acquisition of two residential care homes through Worcester Garden companies in 2002-2003.
Mr Eagles concealed that funding came from his former partner Yvonne's remortgage rather than a 'family trust'.
After relationship breakdown, Mrs Pinfield allotted shares to herself and Mr Eagles filed backdated Companies House forms to regain control.
Mrs Pinfield ran the homes as registered director and responsible person while Mr Eagles faced bankruptcy and creditor pressure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim trial on validity of corporate steps and underlying beneficial ownership of three care home companies.
enrichment.outcome: Fraudulent Companies House steps set aside; self-allotment to Mrs Pinfield set aside; beneficial net equity declared 39% Pinfield and 61% Eagles based on financing contributions.
enrichment.ratio: Where cohabitees embark on a joint commercial venture and one party is encouraged to contribute work and finance on the basis of an equity expectation, Oxley v Hiscock principles may yield a constructive trust share measured by contributions; directors cannot validly allot shares to themselves for an improper purpose without registered shareholder consent.
legal_issues: Whether there was an express agreement for equal shareholding
Constructive trust or proprietary estoppel under Oxley v Hiscock
Validity of backdated filings and share allotments
Fair division of beneficial interest by reference to financing contributions
linked_authorities: Oxley v Hiscock [2004] EWCA Civ 546

confidence.notes: Detailed findings on ownership, corporate invalidity and quantification are clearly recorded.
